pitch_detail.notes: Bushy, lichen-covered rock leads to the vegetated top of a pillar. Protection is hard to find.
Go up hollow flakes slightly left of the dihedral. When the flakes run out, an unprotected traverse of about 15 ft to the right reaches the base of the dihedral. Belay wherever suits.
Follow the corner until the angle eases, then build a belay on any good stance with a fine view.

The dihedral relents in angle. Follow it, then ramble over easy slabs and boulders covered in lichen and through some trees to a small heather shelf. You can belay there and scramble to the top, or reach the real summit by a grubby gully; anchors up there may be hard to build.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with the stated grades; no lengths. No rappels (walk-off descent).

pitch_detail.notes: Blocky, vague terrain with the loosest rock on the route, around 150 ft. Once you are about 100 ft up, drift left. A roof arching leftward over a white slab marks the area; a short but sturdy tree directly left of it is the best place to stop.

Sustained 5.7 with a few harder moves, about 190 ft: left-facing corner after left-facing corner. Continue past a yellow and black vertically striped wall on your left, and belay at the tree just above it.

About 170 ft. Rejoin the last left-facing corner on your right, which is a move or two of 5.8, and climb about 30 ft to a friendly ledge with many trees. Then 5.0 scrambling, straight up, and a flume of 5.6 friction and stemming to a live tree, just before the rope runs out.

A rope-stretcher of about 195 ft. Moderate, rambling climbing straight up past many trees; starts at 5.6 and eases to 5.4. Exactly where you stop is not important, only that you aim for the distinctive skewer-shaped tree visible above.

About 150 ft. From the P4 belay look up and right for a tree whose trunk is bare with a ball of foliage partway up. Go up and right through small cracks in little corners, with a few friction moves. For the last 40 ft or so, stay left in the final right-facing corner and climb it directly; it has cleaned up to a sustained 5.8, and the right-hand line through brush is not recommended for rockfall. Belay and partner can see one another all the way.

About 100 ft; rope drag builds, so extend gear well, with short draws on the bolts and double runners on cams. Start from the tree below a looming headwall: climb onto a white block, put a small cam in the horizontal crack at eye level, then go up and left into the clamshell to the first bolt. Skip more gear around there, as the blocks are doubtful. Traverse out left to the second bolt (the crux move comes as you pull above the first bolt), then friction straight up or on the left edge. After brief scrambling go up and right, then make a big step left under a small roof into a horizontal crack (a 5.7 moment, #0.75 or #1). Place gear far left in the crack. Belay on the two bolts next to the base of the P7 crack.

About 100 ft. Take the obvious vertical crack right of the blank headwall. It begins as two offwidth cracks with a fin between, with a stiff first move, then narrows to secure jamming up to a room-sized alcove under a large roof. Belay near the corner to the right without blocking it. A 60 m rope will not link this pitch with P8.

About 120 ft. A fine right-facing corner with a hand-size crack in its depths and small foot ledges off to the sides. Top out far enough into scrambling terrain to be comfortable unroping, and build the last anchor from any of many options.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches. Pitch lengths are written as approximate (about N ft) in the source so they are in notes, not lengthM. Several pitches may be split in the middle for extra belays. No rappels (long walk-off, about 1000 ft of descent).
review.other_findings: Stored length 305 m vs roughly 1,175 ft (about 358 m) summed from pitch lengths.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb about 60 ft of 4th class up a corner to the base of a steep inverted-V crack system. Follow these cracks on hidden holds directly to a good belay ledge.

Climb a low-angle groove with sparse protection to the base of a black slab. Clip a bolt, then either step right around the orange overhang (5.6) or go up left on a thin flake (5.8) and return right to the same spot. Next, relocate the belay up and over the little bowl of loose 3rd class ground, and set a gear belay at the foot of the intimidating finger crack in its upper left.

A short, steep finger crack (5.11-) is the crux, followed by the vertical face above on gear and bolts at 5.10-. You can skip the crux entirely by taking enjoyable 5.8 ground on the left before rejoining the face.
Easy face climbing leads to a steep wide-hands crack and the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches; P3 grade is 5.11- on the crack or 5.10- if the crux is bypassed. Descent is a rappel of the route on a single 60 m rope with no station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep snow heading northeast; stop under a bulge on the right side.
More steep northeast snow, up to the point where a big gully branches off toward the east.
Head east up the large gully. You may find a few rocks to hook in the snow.
Continue up to just below the ridge crest, about 200 ft north of the summit.
Cross over a small gendarme and continue along the exposed crest to the true summit.

review.changed: Wrote the 5 pitches as described. No grades, lengths or anchors are given, so none written. No rappels.

pitch_detail.notes: Take the obvious wide ice flow up the middle of the west face to a comfortable stance with a belay in good ice. The hardest moves are immediately at the start, roughly 15 ft of truly vertical water ice.
Keep climbing the flows to a last bulge that you can pull directly or avoid by stepping right. Moderate 50 degree snow then leads to trees, where you belay.
Cross the snowfield, bending left as cliffs push you toward a notch. Use rock gear or a snag for the belay. Moving together may be needed.

Cross left onto very steep (60 to 70 degree) snow on the north face, with cliffs below you; sling the scattered little trees for protection. After about 40 to 50 ft of this traverse, find a slot going up through the cliff band, where thin ice may coat a slab. Struggle up deep steep snow to the ridge crest.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches. Descent is a rappel off trees using two 60 m ropes; no station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the right side of the grey incisor, either on the easier ramp or directly in the corner (the corner is dirty and awkward). Mostly easy, with a few awkward moves.

Work up by stemming and face moves to the ear. An unexpectedly easy move rightward puts you on far easier ground along its flank and in the low-angle corner above. Run the rope outside the ear and stop at a big ledge.

Follow the main corner system for about 80 ft, then transfer to a corner on your right and another after it. Cross a slab and downclimb a rubble-filled corner on the right, ending on a good ledge with a solid tree belay. Heather and grass still need clearing.
The thin, wavy corner leads to a roof. Step up and right, clip a bolt, and commit to a short run of tenuous grooves that ends at easier ground. The belay is where the first splitter begins.

pitch_detail.anchor: tree on ledge, then next crack system
pitch_detail.notes: Climb the dog-leg hand-crack splitter for about 60 ft to a tree on a ledge; it can be slippery with lichen inside. Skip the arching crack above, step up right, and cross a ramp for about 15 ft to belay in the next crack system.

Climb easy blocks up and right, then a finger crack on a slab at 5.9. At the overlap, a thin finger crack takes about 10 ft of C1 (possibly 5.12 free), after which steep, easy hand jams follow. Shift right along a ledge to a good belay at the foot of the last crack system.
About 50 ft of steep wall climbing eases onto lower-angle ground and the summit ridge. Some stacked blocks and flakes call for careful handling.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches with stated grades and lengths (feet converted). Descent is rappelling and downclimbing the north ridge, or the west ridge over the summit; no station list so no rappel table. No crux marked.

pitch_detail.notes: Low-angle slab climbing up and left. A short crack reaches a small overlap; save a small piece for the pod at the crux, which needs to be narrower than a C4. Pull the overlap on crimps and a shallow finger pod, continue on slab to a second overlap in a corner, mantle, and keep drifting left to a decent stance beneath a roof.

A thin right-facing corner with stemming and finger cracks reaches a tree. Veer left there, through some tedious underclings, into the clean orange corner; resist staying in it and exit right for the belay.
Face climbing up and right, then good cracks leading back left to a brief finger crack and a tricky mantle. Traverse left to a semi-hanging belay in front of a big flake ramp holding a 4-inch crack.

Go up the big detached flake ramp and 4-inch crack on the left, without placing gear behind the flake; a horizontal on the right takes good gear. Work up the face to a small roof, pull through on good laybacks and jams, climb a short crack, mantle, then lower-angle slab to a ledge in a corner under the zebra corner.

Two options. Option 1 (5.10): a short steep crack, then a thinning low-angle crack beside the zebra stripes and under a roof, and back right on huecos, a horizontal and underclings to a stance. Rope drag is nasty, and an extra short 5.9 pitch of finger cracks, layback moves and a chimney is then needed to reach the tree under the big right-facing corner. Option 2 (5.9): same opening crack, then veer right on a ledge with a big rectangular block, past a tree, up a slab with a #1 in huecos, across a slab to cracks in a shallow corner, up it, then hand cracks leftward under a roof, past a tree, and left into a chimney. The belay is the tree under the large corner.

pitch_detail.belay: Belay near the base of a flaring squeeze chimney, at the top of the pitch.
pitch_detail.notes: About 100 ft of secure, sustained right-facing corner that goes from hands to fingers. A large pine leaning outward near the top is an optional belay. Awkward jams and small roofs lead to the foot of a flaring squeeze chimney. Instead of the chimney you can traverse about 30 ft right and down to the last pitch of a neighboring route.
A squeeze chimney with deep protection, best climbed toward its outside face; hard on a follower wearing a pack. Above, an easy 5th class crack on a slab reaches a good stance.
Low 5th to the summit; exposed enough to stay roped with a short belay to the top, which is a flat mesa.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P8 (stored table held only P6; its grade, length and belay are kept). Pitch 5 has two options with different grades, so no single grade. Existing rappel_detail left alone.
review.other_findings: Pitch 5 option 1 needs an extra short pitch, so the true pitch count can be 9.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a small ledge above the snow or talus and climb the obvious hand-and-finger splitter. After the mantle at its top, pass a tree to another ledge and a short corner, then a chimney leads to the belay. Spare rope can haul shoes and clothing up from the tat on the tree.

Head left via hanging corners and round several aretes to a short wide stretch. Go on up and left over an exposed crack traverse, passing the bolted belay, then left across a slab to a short face crux and further left to a big slung pillar. Some climbers split it for rope management.
Climb the pillar's corner, then launch up and right along an exposed horizontal crack. Belay on a large sloping ledge at its end.
Go up, bend slightly left into a V-slot, and weave left, right, and left again on finger cracks and stems. Watch your rope. The belay is the broad ledge at mid-height of the wall.
Shift the belay 25 ft left to the foot of the striking corner crack. A hard start off the ground leads into the aesthetic corner, which you follow to a good belay ledge.

A corner crack that is stouter than it first looks, mantling to a good ledge, then up the crack onto a slab. Make a right-to-left traverse with sparse protection, continue up a corner crack, and finish just left at a ramp belay.
Continue left on a finger-crack traverse to the major corner system on the left, which has many belay ledges.

The corner system continues for two or three pitches, with an odd 5.10 step. Finish by moving right over easy ground to the headwall's top. A great deal of loose rock lies on the last traverse back right above the headwall, so be very careful.

review.changed: Replaced the single lumped '1-8' entry with P1-P7 plus a combined 8-10, using the stated grades and lengths (the text describes up to 10 pitches). Rappel table already exists, left alone.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count 8; the text describes 10 pitches (P8-10 is 2-3 pitches).

pitch_detail.notes: Snowpack decides the start: hop right into the offwidth, or cross a deep snowfield to join the crack higher up. One continuous crack system runs from tight fingers to wide; tight hands and good footwork pay off. It finishes on a ledge. Extra .4 and .5 cams help on the long pitch.

Walk up from the belay toward a notch gully in the left wall, clipping a pin low down, then place some gear before a few fun moves into the gully. Go up 4th class to a great ledge; this is a short pitch.

Go left from the belay and up a wide box, stepping gently on the red rock, into the right-facing dihedral toward the alcove. Leave the alcove on thin tips and keep climbing until solid hand jams let you trend left on the flakes, up to the roof. The crux is a thin, arching section on small gear onto the Shield, so keep a .2 and your smallest cam in reserve. Finish on a ledge.
Climb the splitter crack to the top of the Shield and a large ledge.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches; all belays are said to be bolted (no counts given). Descent: single 70 m rope rappel, with an intermediate anchor on the ledge left of the route between the P1 anchor and the ground; no full station list so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin at a small dihedral crack, about 15 ft tall, on the right end of the low buttress, then continue up the slab above on scattered cracks.
Third class ground rises to a plateau with small trees; set the belay below the steep headwall.
Climb a ramp that trends left across the middle of the dirty-looking headwall, then head straight up its center, bearing slightly right. Mostly clean rock; loose blocks are the thing to watch.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches. Descent is a walk-off to the right, then down easy slabs to the left; no rappels.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin where the rock has a weakness and a small tree about 15 ft up, then angle left for roughly 150 ft.
Aim for a right-facing corner on thin cracks and bulges for 120 ft. Described as spicy.

Mostly straight up, with a firm leftward traverse across clean slab below stacked blocks, 150 ft in all; this completes the first panel. A downhill walk of about 150 ft takes you to the start of the next pitch.
Aim for the left side of the first bulge and continue to the great headwall, about 170 ft.
Head up avoiding bad rock and manage rope drag. About 160 ft would top out the panel, but drag stopped the first party short.
A brief pitch finishing the panel, right at the mouth of the crack hall.
Good-hands option in the crack hall: steep, clean rock for 150 ft, trending left at the top.
Lower-angle hands trending up and right for 120 ft, with some scrambling to the right.
Fingers and hands in a right-trending crack for 120 ft, ending a bit scrambly.
Mostly scrambling with a few bulges; stay left to avoid the worst rock.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches as listed. Lengths written only where the text states them without 'roughly' or 'about'. Descent is a ridge walk and gully with one rap of about 30 m from a tree, not a station list, so no rappel table. Many alternative lines exist; this is one line.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble up class 4 slabs with limited protection, meandering up and left, right, and left again to build a belay on a small platform left of the open-book gully.

Enter the open-book gully and climb the dihedral and face; the dihedral gives more protection than the runout face. Where the gully bends right, exit left over a chockstone, then climb left and up to a break with a sloping gravel ledge, and anchor with finger-size cams and nuts below the twin cracks, on a one-person block. It can be split with a belay about 30 m up, though this raises rockfall exposure to the belayer.

Take the inset on cracks directly overhead, or skirt it on the right and step back left. Twin cracks with excellent protection and lovely rock run to their top, then the left-facing dihedral; leave it directly or via a rail stepping left. A ramp rising right leads to an anchor beneath the hanging dihedral, or you can set up just left of it so the belayer stays clear of loose rock from the next boulder problem.

A brief boulder problem up the dihedral right over the anchor starts it. Jam and stem a steep corner by some loose blocks, passing a rappel anchor, then up the steeper and widening dihedral to a chockstone. Face-climb over the bulge into a wide right-facing corner, leaving it to the right and then back left to a stance above the dihedral. Cams from #1 and #2 to #4 fit the anchor options well.

Face-climb above the anchor, wandering to find good rock and gear, past a rappel anchor, over heather ledges and between blocks to a large ledge. The belay sits under a sweeping crescent right-facing corner, with hand-size pieces.

pitch_detail.anchor: piton anchor, or crack anchor 30 m higher
pitch_detail.notes: Length 30 to 55 m depending on where you stop. Two short steps and ledges lead to the right-facing corner. Jam it, or use face holds on the right. After exiting the corner, go right then back up and left for the easier way, or go straight up the runout exit. After exiting, belay at a piton anchor (rappel station) or continue up easy runout slab for another 30 m to an anchor in cracks above a shrubby ledge.

25 to 30 m. Continue up a ramp beside a right-facing wall to the corner, climb a couple of loose blocks, and step left. Go up more loose blocks and cross a small roof to the left with big exposure; protection is marginal fingertip size and a fall here is a gamble. Cross the foot rail and belay below a hanging dihedral on finger to hand sizes.

15 to 25 m. Steep finger cracks and face moves climb the hanging dihedral, then off-hands cracks lead out left to easy, runout ground. Stop on a stance using finger-size gear, or carry on up the runout groove to the broad tree ledge. Lichen has made holds greasy.
If you belayed just above the dihedral, the runout slot and groove take you to easier terrain and the big tree ledge.

Follow a loose chimney or gully with gear in the sound rock, and keep drag low; leave on the left through the trees or via rock beside them. A short scramble gets you to the summit, or you can go on north along the summit ridge.

rappel_detail.anchor: slings on the large treed ledge
rappel_detail.station: Large treed ledge at the top of pitch 10.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the bottom of the crux dihedral, where a fixed nut anchor is set. No anchor was left for descending from the top to the treed ledge.
Rappel straight down to a two-piton anchor in the middle of pitch 6.
The next stop is a ledge shortly above the bottom of pitch 6. With a 70 m rope you may manage it in one rappel.

rappel_detail.station: Ledge near the bottom of pitch 6.
rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel across the ledge to the top of pitch 5.
Rappel down through the pitch 4 crux dihedral to a hanging anchor, or instead build a new anchor at the top of pitch 4.
A shorter rappel to the bottom of pitch 4, where fixed tri-cams and cams are in place.

Here you leave the climbing line: rappel the clean slab down and to climber's left. A full-length rappel finishes on slick, exposed heather above a drop, so look for the following anchor on boulders to climber's left, lower down.
Rappel into the chimney. On the first good ledge, peek around the corner on your left to find a protected nut anchor. The pull has loose rock.

rappel_detail.station: Ledge around the corner left of the chimney.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel past a dead tree and down the steep, flaky cracks known as the Piano Keys. The following anchor is down and right, a rope-stretching distance away, and could use small nuts or pitons. Bring a 70 m rope, knot both ends, and mind the pendulum.

rappel_detail.station: Anchor at the end of the Piano Keys rappel.
rappel_detail.notes: The final rappel goes over a roof at the base, another stretch for the rope with a 60 m. Take a 70 m and knot the ends.

review.changed: Wrote all 10 pitches and the 10 listed rappels (a rappel 0 with no anchor is mentioned as unavailable). Several station details are vague and the list was read in the order given; lengths with ranges are in the notes.

pitch_detail.notes: Roughly 700 ft of 4th class and low 5th, with a few steeper steps. Suitable for moving together.
First of the crack-system pitches on excellent rock.
Crack-system climbing on good rock.
Crack-system climbing on good rock.
Crack-system climbing on good rock; this is the hardest pitch of the route.
Crack-system climbing on good rock.
Crack-system climbing on good rock.
Crack-system climbing on good rock.
Two pitches at the same grade that finish on the ridge crest.
An easy but exposed pitch along the crest to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote the pitches as grouped by the text: 1-5 together (700 ft), single pitches 6-12, 13-14 together, and 15. Per-pitch detail beyond grade is not given. No rappel table; descent is a long route with one or two rappels, not listed by station.
